text:
### Observed differences

- In the earlier window, six activities each ran in only about half of the traces: A28, A30 and A31 in about 49 in 100 traces, and A32, A33 and A34 in about 52 in 100. In the later window all six run in about 99 in 100 traces, still at most once per trace in both windows. [OCC001, OCC002, OCC003, OCC004, OCC005, OCC006]
- The two groups of three were mutually exclusive earlier and are executed together later: in the earlier window no trace contained both an activity from the set A28/A30/A31 and one from A32/A33/A34 (co-occurrence 0 of 200 traces; each pair appeared as one-group-only in roughly half of traces each). In the later window every such cross-group pair co-occurs in about 98 in 100 traces. [REL015, REL016, REL017, REL019, REL020, REL021, REL022, REL023, REL024]
- Ordering: in both windows A25 precedes all six activities and all six precede A26 whenever they occur; in the later window the A28/A30/A31 activities precede the A32/A33/A34 activities in about 98 in 100 traces. Within each group of three the order remains mixed (both orders in similar shares) in both windows. [REL001, REL002, REL003, REL004, REL005, REL006, REL007, REL008, REL009, REL010, REL011, REL012, REL013, REL018, REL025, REL026, REL027]
- Event-position gaps widened consistently with the groups being concatenated: the distance from A25 to A32/A33/A34 was 1–3 positions in the earlier window (roughly a third each) and 4–5 positions in the later one (about half each); the same shift appears between A28/A30/A31 and A26. Relative positions moved accordingly: A28/A30/A31 earlier (mean about 0.74 to 0.68), A32/A33/A34 later (about 0.73 to 0.77), A25 slightly earlier (0.67 to 0.62) and A26 slightly later (0.80 to 0.83). [LAG001, LAG002, LAG003, LAG004, LAG005, LAG006, POS001, POS002, POS003, POS004, POS005, POS006, POS007, POS008]
- The pattern is far beyond what screening expects by chance: 47 of 89 tested control-flow units qualified versus roughly 0.44 expected for an unchanged process, and each item's difference exceeds all but about 1 in 200 random re-splits of the pooled data. [OCC001-OCC006, POS001-POS008, REL001-REL027, LAG001-LAG006]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis that an exclusive choice between two blocks of activities was removed, so that both blocks now run in sequence within the same cases. In the earlier window a trace contained A25, then either the block A28/A30/A31 (about 49 in 100 traces) or the block A32/A33/A34 (about 52 in 100), then A26, with the two blocks never appearing together; in the later window nearly every trace contains A25, then A28, A30 and A31 in no fixed order among themselves, then A32, A33 and A34 in no fixed order, then A26. [OCC001, OCC004, REL001, REL007, REL015, REL022, REL025]

The support is direct and consistent: all nine cross-group activity pairs move from never co-occurring to co-occurring in about 98 in 100 traces, participation of all six activities rises from about half of traces to nearly all, and the lag distributions show one block being inserted between A25 and the second group and between the first group and A26. With 47 qualifying items against roughly 0.44 expected without change, chance alone cannot account for the pattern as a whole. [REL015, REL019, REL022, OCC001, LAG001, LAG004]

Limitations: the evidence contains no direct successor information, so the exact adjacency created by joining the blocks is not confirmed, and within-block order stays unfixed in both windows, so the hypothesis concerns block-level concatenation rather than a fixed sequence. A competing explanation the evidence cannot rule out is a shift in case mix, with the later window covering only cases that always required both blocks; the complete absence of co-occurrence earlier (0 of 200 traces) makes a pure sampling artefact implausible, however. [REL013, REL018, REL025]
